canonical_question: Why was the slower cooling rate of 5.42 K/ps tested if the study ultimately adopted the faster rate of 21.11 K/ps for all simulations?

question_variants.question: Why was the slower cooling rate of 5.42 K/ps tested if the study ultimately adopted the faster rate of 21.11 K/ps for all simulations?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The slower cooling rate (5.42 K/ps) was tested to compare structural outcomes with the faster rate (21.11 K/ps) at a fixed temperature. The comparison showed no significant change in the radial distribution function g(r), justifying the adoption of the faster rate for subsequent simulations across the full temperature range.

answers.answer: The study tested two different cooling rates (21.11 K/ps and 5.42 K/ps) to determine if the quenching rate affected the final structure. At 300 K, no significant change was observed in the radial distribution function g(r) for different atomic pairs between the two rates. Consequently, the faster rate of 21.11 K/ps was maintained for all simulations in the study.
answers.measurement_outcome: No significant change in g(r) at 300 K between 5.42 K/ps and 21.11 K/ps
answers.mechanism: Quench rate insensitivity at fixed temperature for structural pair correlations
answers.boundary_limitation: Justification specific to 300 K temperature point
evidence_spans: Using the methods and approximations for accurate estimates of the formation enthalpy and relative energy of A1 and A2 phases [28] , the first-principles KKR-CPA results in Fig. 2 for Al of 0 < x < 2 mole fractions predict a similar global stability found in the experiment, i.e., A1 for x < 0.5, A1 + A2 for 0.5 ≤ Al ≤1.25, and A2 for Al > 1.25.

source_evidence_spans: rapid quenching of the alloy under the NPT ensemble at 0 MPa with two different cooling rates of 21.11 K/ps and 5.42 K/ps, respectively
